new_statements.quote: Comme à travers tout le domaine bantou de la zone C, il existe en ombesa deux tons de base, bas ( ` ) et haut ( ´ ). Leur combinaison engendre des tons complexes, montant et descendant. Pour des raisons d'économie le ton bas n'est pas marqué comme l'indique les exemples cités jusqu'ici. [p. 95] … Les tons ont une valeur lexicale: deux mots segmentairement identiques peuvent avoir deux significations différentes à cause des tons qu'ils portent. [p. 96]
new_statements.translation: As throughout the Bantu domain of zone C, Ombesa has two basic tones, low ( ` ) and high ( ´ ). Their combination produces complex tones, rising and falling. For reasons of economy the low tone is not marked, as the examples cited so far show. … Tones have lexical value: two segmentally identical words can have two different meanings because of the tones they carry.
new_statements.citation: Motingea Mangulu, André. 2012. Contributions aux études linguistiques sur le haut Congo: Esquisses du soa, mbesa, tofoké et lokelé. (ILCAA Language Monograph Series 6.) Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.
new_statements.locator: Chapitre troisième, La langue des Mombesa, §3.2.4 'Tons', pp. 95-96 (part-2 PDF pages 19-20); syllable statement §'Syllabe' p. 96
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mbesa is described as a two-tone register language (H, L, with rising and falling contours) with lexically contrastive tone; the description contains no statement about word stress or accent at all, so no stress position can be assigned from it.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress discussed). Tone-sequence rules (B-B>B, B-H>M, H-B>D, H-H>H), absorption of L by a 'prominent' H in contour simplification, and tonal harmony of prefinal/extension syllables with the final are given in §3.3.3, pp. 100-101.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone; examples are citation forms and short clauses elicited from one speaker (Yandukä group, Yahuma) in 1993. Syllables are open (V, CV, CSV) plus a syllabic nasal in the 1sg recent past (p. 96).
new_statements.identity_note: Motingea Mangulu 2012 (the only real description) covers the Yandukä variety (groupement de Yanduka, secteur Mondimbi, Territoire de Yahuma), one informant from the village of Yamosamba, elicited in Mbandaka in 1993; the author states that the Ikangana speech near Ebonda/Ndobo (Johnston 1919) is a variant of Ombesa (p. 89). De Boeck 1951 worked with speakers from around Bondamba, Yahuma. Glottolog has no separate dialect codes under mbes1238. Mbesa is a tone language (two basic tones, H and L, with contour tones); no source says anything about word stress.

sources.note: Chapter 3 'La langue des Mombesa' (pp. 88-137), section 3.2 'Phonétique et phonologie' (pp. 89-96) treats vowels, semivowels, consonants, tones ('3.2.4. Tons', p. 95-96: two basic tones L and H, complex rising/falling tones, lexical tone with minimal pairs) and the syllable (p. 96: open syllables V, CV, CSV plus syllabic N in 1sg recent past); 3.3.3 'Morphotonèmes' (pp. 100-101) gives tone-sequence rules. Nothing on stress/accent anywhere in the Mbesa chapter (scanned of pp. 77-136 greps clean for accent/intensité/stress/proéminence except 'le haut qui est proéminent' about tone absorption, p…

sources.citation: Grégoire, Claire. 2003. The Bantu languages of the forest. In Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, ch. 19, pp. 349-370. London: Routledge.
sources.note: Areal survey; cites Mbesa (C51) for NC-sequence reductions (nímà 'ape', kòì 'leopard', sòkù 'elephant', p. 356) and for class 2/6 prefix merger (p. 360, 369). Tone discussion (p. 358) is generic for zone C (two register tones plus contour tones); no statement about stress in Mbesa or C50.

sources.citation: De Boeck, L. B. 1951. Een greep uit de Mombesa-taal. Aequatoria 14: 136-143.
sources.note: Eight-page note (wordlist + grammatical observations) from a few days' elicitation; footnote 1 (p. 136) says tones are marked in places as h(oog), l(aag), s(tijgend), with the trema for the middle tone; tone contrasts on adjective/genitive/relative prefixes are discussed (pp. 139-142). No mention of klemtoon/accent/stress. Volume PDF has a text layer.
